claim: Many plants attract and reward pollinators with floral scents and nectar, respectively.
source: Many plants attract and reward pollinators with floral scents and nectar, respectively, but these traits can also incur fitness costs as they also attract herbivores.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant-pollinator interactions that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Floral scents and nectar can incur fitness costs by attracting herbivores.
source: Many plants attract and reward pollinators with floral scents and nectar, respectively, but these traits can also incur fitness costs as they also attract herbivores.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge and is tested in the manuscript.

claim: Both nectar and scent are highly variable in native populations of Nicotiana attenuata.
source: Both nectar and scent are highly variable in native populations of coyote tobacco, Nicotiana attenuata, with some producing no nectar at all, uncorrelated with the tobacco's main floral attractant, benzylacetone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements presented in Figure 1.

claim: Some Nicotiana attenuata plants produce no nectar at all.
source: Both nectar and scent are highly variable in native populations of coyote tobacco, Nicotiana attenuata, with some producing no nectar at all, uncorrelated with the tobacco's main floral attractant, benzylacetone.
evidence: This is supported by data showing nectar-free plants in the screening experiments.

claim: Nectar production is uncorrelated with benzylacetone emission in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: Both nectar and scent are highly variable in native populations of coyote tobacco, Nicotiana attenuata, with some producing no nectar at all, uncorrelated with the tobacco's main floral attractant, benzylacetone.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing no linear relationship between BA emission and nectar volume.

claim: Both scent and nectar increase outcrossing rates for three separately tested pollinators.
source: Both scent and nectar increase outcrossing rates for three, separately tested, pollinators and both traits increase oviposition by a hawkmoth herbivore, with nectar being more influential than scent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from pollination assays with M. sexta, H. lineata, and A. alexandri.

claim: Both scent and nectar increase oviposition by a hawkmoth herbivore.
source: Both scent and nectar increase outcrossing rates for three, separately tested, pollinators and both traits increase oviposition by a hawkmoth herbivore, with nectar being more influential than scent.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from field and tent experiments.

claim: Nectar is more influential than scent in increasing oviposition by hawkmoth herbivores.
source: Both scent and nectar increase outcrossing rates for three, separately tested, pollinators and both traits increase oviposition by a hawkmoth herbivore, with nectar being more influential than scent.
evidence: This is supported by comparative oviposition data showing stronger effects of nectar absence.

claim: Plants attract pollinators to move pollen from one flower to another to ensure outcrossing.
source: Plants attract pollinators to move pollen from one flower to another to ensure outcrossing and frequently pay for these pollination services by rewarding floral visitors with nectar (Kevan and Baker, 1983; Schemske and Bradshaw, 1999; Raguso and Willis, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Plants frequently pay for pollination services by rewarding floral visitors with nectar.
source: Plants attract pollinators to move pollen from one flower to another to ensure outcrossing and frequently pay for these pollination services by rewarding floral visitors with nectar (Kevan and Baker, 1983; Schemske and Bradshaw, 1999; Raguso and Willis, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Rewardless flowers have evolved in all major groups of angiosperms.
source: Even though it is clear that both floral scent and nectar provide fitness benefits for plants, rewardless flowers have evolved in all major groups of angiosperms (Renner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Renner, 2006.

claim: Orchids have frequently evolved deceptive pollination systems.
source: Orchids, in particular, have frequently evolved deceptive pollination systems, in which flowers attract pollinators by mimicking mating partners or oviposition sites without offering rewards (Schiestl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schiestl, 2005.

claim: Rewardless, nectar-free flowers are commonly found within species that normally provide nectar.
source: But rewardless, nectar-free, flowers are commonly found within species that normally provide nectar, and this is surprising, as the occasional nectar-free flowers would have a disadvantage if visitors have the sensory abilities to avoid rewardless flowers (Karban, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Karban, 2015.

claim: Most flowers hide their rewards deep in the corolla tube.
source: Early on, theorists (Bell, 1986) recognized that most flowers hide their rewards, for example, deep in the corolla tube, which thwarts the easy visual evaluation of a flower's standing nectar volume and developed an ESS model for the proportion of cheating flowers and discriminating visitors that would be evolutionarily stable.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bell, 1986.

claim: Nectar secretion is highly variable within plants of a population.
source: Gilbert et al. (1991) found that nectar secretion was highly variable within plants of a population and suggested that floral visitors could distinguish between low and high nectar secreting plants.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gilbert et al., 1991.

claim: Hawkmoth pollinators can use humidity as a proxy for the presence of nectar.
source: Recent research suggests that hawkmoth pollinators can use humidity as a proxy for the presence of nectar (von Arx et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to von Arx et al., 2012.

claim: Pollinators avoided inflorescences with greater numbers of empty flowers.
source: Ishii et al. (2008) found that pollinators avoided inflorescences with greater numbers of empty flowers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ishii et al., 2008.

claim: Nectar-deficient Petunia lines produced fewer seeds than nectar-replete control plants.
source: Brandenburg et al. (2012a) found that nectar-deficient Petunia lines produced fewer seeds than did nectar-replete control plants, because Manduca sexta moths reduced their probing times in low-nectar plants, which in turn, reduced pollen transfer and thus seed set.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brandenburg et al., 2012a.

claim: Floral scent plays a central role in attracting insect pollinators to flowers.
source: Floral scent is known to play a central role in attracting insect pollinators to flowers (Galen and Newport, 1988; Jürgens et al., 2002; Klahre et al., 2011; Byers et al., 2014; Riffell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Benzylacetone emission is required to maximize both maternal and paternal fitness in Nicotiana attenuata in the field.
source: Kessler et al. (2008) genetically manipulated the biosynthesis of the most abundant floral volatile, benzylacetone (BA), in the flowers of the wild tobacco (Nicotiana attenuata) to demonstrate that BA emission is required to maximize both maternal and paternal fitness in the field when the entire native community of floral visitors had access to the flowers.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler et al., 2008.

claim: Floral scents allow florivores to locate their host plants.
source: Floral scents allow florivores to locate their host plants (Theis, 2006; Theis and Adler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Theis, 2006 and Theis and Adler, 2012.

claim: Individual compounds in floral scent bouquets can specifically deter florivores and nectar robbers.
source: Several studies have shown that individual compounds in floral scent bouquets specifically deter florivores and nectar robbers (Galen et al., 2011; Junker et al., 2011; Kessler et al., 2013) and thus complex floral scents can both attract pollinators and deter antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Nectar addition increased oviposition by Manduca sexta in Datura wrightii.
source: In both Datura wrightii (Adler and Bronstein, 2004), as well as N. attenuata (Kessler, 2012) nectar addition increased oviposition by M. sexta, a pollinator as an adult as well as a devastating herbivore as a caterpillar for both plant species.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Adler and Bronstein, 2004.

claim: Nectar addition increased oviposition by Manduca sexta in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: In both Datura wrightii (Adler and Bronstein, 2004), as well as N. attenuata (Kessler, 2012) nectar addition increased oviposition by M. sexta, a pollinator as an adult as well as a devastating herbivore as a caterpillar for both plant species.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler, 2012.

claim: The average standing nectar volume in sampled Nicotiana attenuata plants was 3.3 μL.
source: The average standing nectar volume was 3.3 μL and varied between single genotypes between 1.3 μL and 5.7 μL per flower (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Standing nectar volume varied between 1.3 μL and 5.7 μL per flower among Nicotiana attenuata genotypes.
source: The average standing nectar volume was 3.3 μL and varied between single genotypes between 1.3 μL and 5.7 μL per flower (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: The average benzylacetone emission was 5.0 ng per flower per night in sampled Nicotiana attenuata plants.
source: The average emission was 5.0 ng BA per flower per night, varying between a minimum emission of 0.5 ng and a maximum of 33.9 ng, equivalent to a 70-fold difference in emission rates (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Benzylacetone emission varied between 0.5 ng and 33.9 ng per flower per night among Nicotiana attenuata genotypes.
source: The average emission was 5.0 ng BA per flower per night, varying between a minimum emission of 0.5 ng and a maximum of 33.9 ng, equivalent to a 70-fold difference in emission rates (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nectar sugar concentration varied between 14.6 and 22.8% in newly opened Nicotiana attenuata flowers.
source: Sugar concentration in newly opened flowers varied between 14.6 and 22.8%, with an average of 18.2%.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of nectar sugar concentration.

claim: Two Nicotiana attenuata plants out of 424 screened produced no nectar at all.
source: Of these, two plants produced no nectar at all.
evidence: This is supported by screening data from 424 plants.

claim: The lack of nectar production in lines 83 and 84 was heritable.
source: These lines (83 and 84) were inbred for two generations and plants of the T2 generations of both lines also did not produce any nectar in any flowers at all stages of development (Figure 1), demonstrating that the lack of nectar production was heritable.
evidence: This is supported by data from inbred generations shown in Figure 1.

claim: All flowers from all 424 screened Nicotiana attenuata plants produced benzylacetone in some measurable quantity.
source: All flowers from all 424 plants in this analysis produced BA in some measureable quantity.
evidence: This is supported by screening data.

claim: There is no linear correlation between benzylacetone emission and nectar volume in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: We found no evidence for a linear correlation between BA emission and nectar volume (y = 0.1875x + 1.02, R2 = 0.01), BA emission and nectar sugar concentration (y = 0.1233x + 3.89, R2 = 0.01), or nectar volume and nectar sugar (y = −1.4471x + 22.99, R2 = 0.41).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis with R2 = 0.01.

claim: There is no linear correlation between benzylacetone emission and nectar sugar concentration in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: We found no evidence for a linear correlation between BA emission and nectar volume (y = 0.1875x + 1.02, R2 = 0.01), BA emission and nectar sugar concentration (y = 0.1233x + 3.89, R2 = 0.01), or nectar volume and nectar sugar (y = −1.4471x + 22.99, R2 = 0.41).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis with R2 = 0.01.

claim: CHAL plants produced only 22.9% of the seeds produced by EV plants when exposed to all natural pollinators.
source: CHAL plants produced only 22.9% (p < 0.001), Sweet9 9.7% (p < 0.001), and CHALxSWEET9 11.6% (p < 0.001) of the seeds produced by EV from outcrossed pollen.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from field experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SWEET9 plants produced only 9.7% of the seeds produced by EV plants when exposed to all natural pollinators.
source: CHAL plants produced only 22.9% (p < 0.001), Sweet9 9.7% (p < 0.001), and CHALxSWEET9 11.6% (p < 0.001) of the seeds produced by EV from outcrossed pollen.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from field experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants produced only 11.6% of the seeds produced by EV plants when exposed to all natural pollinators.
source: CHAL plants produced only 22.9% (p < 0.001), Sweet9 9.7% (p < 0.001), and CHALxSWEET9 11.6% (p < 0.001) of the seeds produced by EV from outcrossed pollen.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from field experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The most frequent floral visitors of Nicotiana attenuata at night in the field were Manduca sexta, Manduca quinquemaculata, and Hyles lineata hawkmoths.
source: The most frequent floral visitors of N. attenuata at night in the field at the time of the experiment were M. sexta, Manduca quinquemaculata, and Hyles lineata hawkmoths (Sphingidae), and Archilochus alexandri hummingbirds (Trochilidae) during the day time.
evidence: This is based on field observations during the experiments.

claim: Archilochus alexandri hummingbirds were the most frequent daytime floral visitors of Nicotiana attenuata in the field.
source: The most frequent floral visitors of N. attenuata at night in the field at the time of the experiment were M. sexta, Manduca quinquemaculata, and Hyles lineata hawkmoths (Sphingidae), and Archilochus alexandri hummingbirds (Trochilidae) during the day time.
evidence: This is based on field observations during the experiments.

claim: CHAL plants produced 75.6% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated exclusively by hummingbirds.
source: While CHAL (75.6%; Friedman signed rank test χ2 = 7.66, df = 2, n = 24, p = 0.02; p = 0.835) plants produced almost as many seeds as EV plant, SWEET9 plants produced considerably fewer seeds than did EV plants (13.1%; p = 0.074) and significantly fewer seeds than did CHAL plants (17.4%; p = 0.005; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from hummingbird-only pollination experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SWEET9 plants produced 13.1% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated exclusively by hummingbirds.
source: While CHAL (75.6%; Friedman signed rank test χ2 = 7.66, df = 2, n = 24, p = 0.02; p = 0.835) plants produced almost as many seeds as EV plant, SWEET9 plants produced considerably fewer seeds than did EV plants (13.1%; p = 0.074) and significantly fewer seeds than did CHAL plants (17.4%; p = 0.005; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from hummingbird-only pollination experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SWEET9 plants produced only 44.6% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Manduca sexta individuals.
source: Although SWEET9 lines produced only 44.6% of the seeds produced by EV plants (p = 0.006), the avoidance of plants which produce no floral scent had an even stronger effect on seed set.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from M. sexta pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CHAL plants produced only 17.4% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Manduca sexta individuals.
source: CHAL plants produced only 17.4% of the seeds of EV (p < 0.001), just as CHALxSWEET9 plants which produced only 5.2% of the seeds produced by EV plants (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from M. sexta pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants produced only 5.2% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Manduca sexta individuals.
source: CHAL plants produced only 17.4% of the seeds of EV (p < 0.001), just as CHALxSWEET9 plants which produced only 5.2% of the seeds produced by EV plants (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from M. sexta pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CHAL plants produced 96.6% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Hyles lineata individuals.
source: Both CHAL (96.6%; p = 0.853) and SWEET9 (111.69%; p = 0.578) plants produced a number of seeds equivalent to those of EV plants.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from H. lineata pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SWEET9 plants produced 111.69% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Hyles lineata individuals.
source: Both CHAL (96.6%; p = 0.853) and SWEET9 (111.69%; p = 0.578) plants produced a number of seeds equivalent to those of EV plants.
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from H. lineata pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants produced only 21.3% of the seeds produced by EV plants when pollinated by single Hyles lineata individuals.
source: Only when the flowers lacked both floral traits (CHALxSWEET9) was seed set mediated by H. lineata pollinator activity significantly reduced (21.3%; p = 0.003).
evidence: This is supported by seed production data from H. lineata pollination experiments in the tent shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CHAL plants received only 43.1% of the eggs found on EV plants in the field.
source: On CHAL plants, only 43.1% (p = 0.046) of the eggs found on EV plants were oviposited.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from field experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: SWEET9 plants received only 10.8% of the eggs found on EV plants in the field.
source: The effect was even stronger in plants unable to produce nectar (SWEET9, 10.8%; CHALxSWEET9, 6.5%, p = 0.046).
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from field experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants received only 6.5% of the eggs found on EV plants in the field.
source: The effect was even stronger in plants unable to produce nectar (SWEET9, 10.8%; CHALxSWEET9, 6.5%, p = 0.046).
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from field experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CHAL plants received 81.9% of the eggs of EV plants in tent experiments with single Manduca sexta moths.
source: CHAL plants received only 81.9% (p = 0.096) of the eggs of EV plants, while SWEET9 received 52.5% (p = 0.058) and CHALxSWEET9 received 48.4% (p = 0.007) of eggs compared with EV.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from tent experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: SWEET9 plants received 52.5% of the eggs of EV plants in tent experiments with single Manduca sexta moths.
source: CHAL plants received only 81.9% (p = 0.096) of the eggs of EV plants, while SWEET9 received 52.5% (p = 0.058) and CHALxSWEET9 received 48.4% (p = 0.007) of eggs compared with EV.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from tent experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants received 48.4% of the eggs of EV plants in tent experiments with single Manduca sexta moths.
source: CHAL plants received only 81.9% (p = 0.096) of the eggs of EV plants, while SWEET9 received 52.5% (p = 0.058) and CHALxSWEET9 received 48.4% (p = 0.007) of eggs compared with EV.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from tent experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No differences in oviposition were found between different lines in the non-flowering stage.
source: In the non-flowering stage, no differences in oviposition were found between the different lines (Friedman signed rank test χ2 = 2.81, df = 3, n = 6, p = 0.4214).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with non-flowering plants.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata is a self-compatible plant.
source: N. attenuata is capable of producing the full set of seeds of comparable mass and number from self-pollination as from outcrossing (Baldwin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baldwin et al., 1997.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata can produce the full set of seeds from self-pollination as from outcrossing.
source: N. attenuata is capable of producing the full set of seeds of comparable mass and number from self-pollination as from outcrossing (Baldwin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baldwin et al., 1997.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata seeds can spend hundreds of years in the seed bank before germinating.
source: Given that N. attenuata seeds can spend hundreds of years in the seed bank before germinating (Preston and Baldwin, 1999), outcrossing will likely be associated with longevity in the seedbank.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Preston and Baldwin, 1999.

claim: Outcrossing is thought to increase herbivore resistance in future generations.
source: In other systems outcrossing is thought to increase herbivore resistance in future generations (Bello-Bedoy and Núnez-Farfán, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bello-Bedoy and Núnez-Farfán, 2011.

claim: Archilochus alexandri visits Nicotiana attenuata approximately 2 hours before dusk until dusk and again in the morning after dawn for 2 hours.
source: A. alexandri visits N. attenuata approximately 2 h before dusk until dusk and again in the morning after dawn for 2 h.
evidence: This is based on field observations.

claim: Hyles lineata visits Nicotiana attenuata from 1 hour before dusk until 1 hour after dawn.
source: H. lineata visits from 1 h before dusk until 1 h after dawn, and finally both Manduca species pollinate and oviposit after dusk until dawn, with periods of enhanced activity depending on moonlight, temperature, and other conditions.
evidence: This is based on field observations.

claim: Both Manduca species pollinate and oviposit after dusk until dawn.
source: H. lineata visits from 1 h before dusk until 1 h after dawn, and finally both Manduca species pollinate and oviposit after dusk until dawn, with periods of enhanced activity depending on moonlight, temperature, and other conditions.
evidence: This is based on field observations.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata flowers secrete nectar slowly over the night until approximately 4 am.
source: N. attenuata flowers secrete nectar slowly over the night until approximately 4 am (Kessler, 2012), theoretically keeping a low but constant amount of nectar over the entire night, even if floral visitors removed the majority of nectar in the dusk or in the first half of the night.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler, 2012.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata produces tiny amounts of nectar in comparison to other sympatric plant species that compete for Manduca sexta's pollination services.
source: Indeed N. attenuata produces tiny amounts of nectar in comparison to other sympatric plant species that compete for M. sexta's pollination services (Raguso et al., 2003; Riffell et al., 2008), and thus seems to have optimized the attractant–reward proportions to maximize its fitness when dealing with this pollinator which is also an herbivore, albeit at a different life stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raguso et al., 2003 and Riffell et al., 2008.

claim: Datura wrightii accumulates 20 times more nectar than Nicotiana attenuata.
source: D. wrightii, for example, a plant which shares M. sexta as both pollinator and herbivore, is a perennial plant that accumulates 20 times more nectar, produces a large amount of foliage that allows it to better compensate for losses to herbivores, and recruits fewer pollinating species than does N. attenuata (Kessler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler, 2012.

claim: Hyles lineata moves sequentially from one flower to the next, visiting all flowers within one inflorescence.
source: While H. lineata moves sequentially from one flower to the next—visiting all flowers within one inflorescence (even visiting the same flower multiple times)—and from one plant to the next plant, both Manduca species visit only a few flowers within an inflorescence before moving on and skipping as many as 10 intervening plants (personal observations).
evidence: This is based on personal observations by the authors.

claim: Both Manduca species visit only a few flowers within an inflorescence before moving on and skipping as many as 10 intervening plants.
source: While H. lineata moves sequentially from one flower to the next—visiting all flowers within one inflorescence (even visiting the same flower multiple times)—and from one plant to the next plant, both Manduca species visit only a few flowers within an inflorescence before moving on and skipping as many as 10 intervening plants (personal observations).
evidence: This is based on personal observations by the authors.

claim: All four transformed lines were equally able to produce seeds from hand-pollinated flowers.
source: In a control experiment in the tent, all four lines used in the experiments were equally able to produce seeds from hand-pollinated flowers (one-way ANOVA: F3, 36 = 1.19, p = 0.33; n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with hand pollination.

claim: EV plants produced on average 233 ± 23 seeds per flower from hand pollination.
source: EV plants produced on average 233 ± 23 seeds per flower, CHAL 242 ± 22, SWEET9 209 ± 21, and CHALxSWEET9 265 ± 19.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with hand pollination.

claim: CHAL plants produced on average 242 ± 22 seeds per flower from hand pollination.
source: EV plants produced on average 233 ± 23 seeds per flower, CHAL 242 ± 22, SWEET9 209 ± 21, and CHALxSWEET9 265 ± 19.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with hand pollination.

claim: SWEET9 plants produced on average 209 ± 21 seeds per flower from hand pollination.
source: EV plants produced on average 233 ± 23 seeds per flower, CHAL 242 ± 22, SWEET9 209 ± 21, and CHALxSWEET9 265 ± 19.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with hand pollination.

claim: CHALxSWEET9 plants produced on average 265 ± 19 seeds per flower from hand pollination.
source: EV plants produced on average 233 ± 23 seeds per flower, CHAL 242 ± 22, SWEET9 209 ± 21, and CHALxSWEET9 265 ± 19.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments with hand pollination.

claim: Floral scent is an essential floral cue for Manduca sexta.
source: While floral scent is an essential floral cue for M. sexta, it is clearly not for H. lineata.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential seed set results between CHAL and EV plants for M. sexta pollination.

claim: Floral scent is not an essential floral cue for Hyles lineata.
source: While floral scent is an essential floral cue for M. sexta, it is clearly not for H. lineata.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set results showing H. lineata pollinated CHAL plants as effectively as EV plants.

claim: Nectar is essential for pollination by Archilochus alexandri.
source: While nectar is essential for pollination by A. alexandri, the lack of nectar does not reduce the pollination services provided by H. lineata visitations.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set results showing SWEET9 plants had reduced seed set when pollinated by hummingbirds.

claim: The lack of nectar does not reduce the pollination services provided by Hyles lineata.
source: While nectar is essential for pollination by A. alexandri, the lack of nectar does not reduce the pollination services provided by H. lineata visitations.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set results showing SWEET9 plants produced equivalent seeds to EV plants when pollinated by H. lineata.

claim: Plants unable to produce nectar produced more than twice as many seeds as plants unable to produce floral scent when pollinated by Manduca sexta.
source: Although all lines lacking a certain floral trait showed reduced seed set, plants unable to produce nectar still produced more than twice as many seeds than plants unable to produce floral scent.
evidence: This is supported by comparing seed set data between SWEET9 (44.6%) and CHAL (17.4%) plants in M. sexta pollination experiments.

claim: Both floral scent attraction and nectar reward are important to maximize outcrossing by Manduca sexta.
source: However, for the more specialized pollinator, M. sexta, both floral scent attraction and nectar reward are important to maximize outcrossing.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set data showing both CHAL and SWEET9 plants had reduced seed set compared to EV plants.

claim: Hummingbirds may use olfaction and nectar scent to locate nectar sources.
source: Another hypothesis could be that hummingbirds also use olfaction and are able to use nectar scent to locate a proper nectar source.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain why hummingbirds were less attracted to CHAL plants.

claim: Birds use scent in homing and navigation.
source: Birds, long suspected to use scent in homing and navigation (Keeton, 1974) have recently been suggested to use scent for prey localization (Mantyla et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Keeton, 1974 and Mantyla et al., 2008.

claim: Hummingbirds have smaller territories than hawkmoths and pollinate flowers only in a small area close to their nests.
source: Hummingbirds, in contrast to hawkmoths, have smaller territories and pollinate flowers only in a small area close to their nests (Norton et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Norton et al., 1982.

claim: Hummingbirds can learn cues and plant positions correlated with the presence of food sources.
source: This allows them to learn cues and plant positions which are correlated with the presence of food sources (Ackerman et al., 1994; Campbell et al., 1997; Hurly and Healy, 2002) or even with the quality of the food (Pérez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Large hawkmoths like Manduca sexta cover much larger distances each night than hummingbirds.
source: In contrast to hummingbirds, large hawkmoths like M. sexta cover much larger distances each night and rely more on direct perception rather than memory in visiting their food sources (Raguso and Willis, 2003, 2005), as they most likely never visit the same plant twice in nature, although moths are also known to learn when exploring new food sources (Riffell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raguso and Willis, 2003, 2005.

claim: Manduca sexta most likely never visits the same plant twice in nature.
source: In contrast to hummingbirds, large hawkmoths like M. sexta cover much larger distances each night and rely more on direct perception rather than memory in visiting their food sources (Raguso and Willis, 2003, 2005), as they most likely never visit the same plant twice in nature, although moths are also known to learn when exploring new food sources (Riffell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the large distances covered by M. sexta.

claim: Moths are known to learn when exploring new food sources.
source: In contrast to hummingbirds, large hawkmoths like M. sexta cover much larger distances each night and rely more on direct perception rather than memory in visiting their food sources (Raguso and Willis, 2003, 2005), as they most likely never visit the same plant twice in nature, although moths are also known to learn when exploring new food sources (Riffell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riffell et al., 2013.

claim: The pollination assays were conducted with naive moths that lacked experience with rewardless and scentless Nicotiana attenuata plants.
source: The pollination assays were conducted with naive moths that lacked experience with rewardless and scentless N. attenuata plants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the pollination assays.

claim: Experienced Hyles lineata might behave differently than naive moths.
source: Experienced H. lineata might have behaved differently, as has been shown in orchid pollinating bumblebees which were able to learn to avoid deceptive orchids (Internicola and Harder, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation to Internicola and Harder, 2012.

claim: Bumblebees can learn to avoid deceptive orchids.
source: Experienced H. lineata might have behaved differently, as has been shown in orchid pollinating bumblebees which were able to learn to avoid deceptive orchids (Internicola and Harder, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Internicola and Harder, 2012.

claim: Nectar seems to play a larger role than floral scent in Manduca sexta host choice for oviposition.
source: Although, plants unable to produce floral scent had a significantly lower chance of receiving an egg from M. sexta, nectar seems to play a larger role in host choice.
evidence: This is inferred from the oviposition data showing stronger effects of nectar absence than scent absence.

claim: It is the reward more than the attractant which influences female hawkmoth oviposition decisions.
source: It is intriguing that it is the reward more than the attractant which influences the female hawkmoth's oviposition decisions, while the attractant plays a similar role as the reward when the same species is acting as a pollinator.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the relative effects of nectar and scent on oviposition versus pollination.

claim: Moths would learn to avoid floral advertisements if they are not associated with a reward.
source: Similarly, moths would learn to avoid floral advertisements if they are not associated with a reward (Haber, 1984; Smithson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haber, 1984 and Smithson, 2001.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata should minimize nectar accumulation while maximizing floral scent emission to maximize fitness in interactions with Manduca sexta.
source: In an evolutionary context, our findings suggest that for an interaction with M. sexta, N. attenuata plants should minimize their nectar accumulation while maximizing their floral scent emission in order to maximize fitness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trade-off between attracting pollinators and avoiding herbivores.

claim: Nicotiana attenuata produces tiny amounts of nectar compared to other sympatric plant species competing for Manduca sexta pollination services.
source: Indeed N. attenuata produces tiny amounts of nectar in comparison to other sympatric plant species that compete for M. sexta's pollination services (Raguso et al., 2003; Riffell et al., 2008), and thus seems to have optimized the attractant–reward proportions to maximize its fitness when dealing with this pollinator which is also an herbivore, albeit at a different life stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raguso et al., 2003 and Riffell et al., 2008.

claim: Datura wrightii is a perennial plant that produces a large amount of foliage allowing it to better compensate for losses to herbivores.
source: D. wrightii, for example, a plant which shares M. sexta as both pollinator and herbivore, is a perennial plant that accumulates 20 times more nectar, produces a large amount of foliage that allows it to better compensate for losses to herbivores, and recruits fewer pollinating species than does N. attenuata (Kessler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler, 2012.

claim: Datura wrightii recruits fewer pollinating species than Nicotiana attenuata.
source: D. wrightii, for example, a plant which shares M. sexta as both pollinator and herbivore, is a perennial plant that accumulates 20 times more nectar, produces a large amount of foliage that allows it to better compensate for losses to herbivores, and recruits fewer pollinating species than does N. attenuata (Kessler, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessler, 2012.

claim: Pollination success of Nicotiana attenuata is ensured by recruiting several pollinator species.
source: Pollination success of N. attenuata is ensured by recruiting several pollinator species, which may influence the evolution of floral scent and nectar reward.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing multiple pollinator species contribute to seed set.

claim: Hyles lineata provides adequate pollination services without requiring an attractive signal or reward if plants are surrounded by other nectar and scent producing plants.
source: H. lineata also provides adequate pollination services, but without apparent evolutionary pressure on these N. attenuata floral traits, as this species seems to require neither an attractive signal nor a reward, at least if these plants are surrounded by other nectar and scent producing plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set data showing H. lineata pollinated CHAL and SWEET9 plants as effectively as EV plants.

claim: Hyles lineata is not an herbivore on Nicotiana attenuata during its larval stage.
source: Moreover H. lineata is also not an herbivore on N. attenuata during its larval stage.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on knowledge of H. lineata biology.

claim: Only Manduca sexta seems to rely on floral cues and distinguishes between honest and cheating plants in a mixed Nicotiana attenuata population.
source: Only M. sexta seems to rely on the cues provided by the flower and distinguishes between honest and cheating plants in a mixed N. attenuata population.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses of the three pollinators to scent and nectar manipulations.

claim: For Hyles lineata, either floral scent or nectar is sufficient to provide full pollination services.
source: For H. lineata, either floral scent or nectar is sufficient for the moth to provide full pollination services.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set data showing H. lineata pollinated both CHAL and SWEET9 plants as effectively as EV plants.

claim: The honesty of a floral signal plays a key role in plant attractiveness to bee pollinators in Brassica rapa.
source: In bee pollinated Brassica rapa plants, the honesty of a floral signal—that a certain scent would consistently lead to a reward—plays a key role in the plants attractiveness to pollinators (Knauer and Schiestl, 2015), something which seems not to be the case for N. attenuata and its pollinators, as we found no association between BA emission and nectar volume, or nectar sugar concentration.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Knauer and Schiestl, 2015.

claim: There is no association between benzylacetone emission and nectar volume or nectar sugar concentration in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: In bee pollinated Brassica rapa plants, the honesty of a floral signal—that a certain scent would consistently lead to a reward—plays a key role in the plants attractiveness to pollinators (Knauer and Schiestl, 2015), something which seems not to be the case for N. attenuata and its pollinators, as we found no association between BA emission and nectar volume, or nectar sugar concentration.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis showing no linear relationship.

claim: There is a trade-off between rewarding pollinators and avoiding herbivores in the evolution of floral nectar in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: Our data are consistent with a trade-off between rewarding pollinators and avoiding herbivores in the evolution of floral nectar in N. attenuata, but why is BA emission so variable?
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing nectar increases both pollination and oviposition.

claim: Increasing floral scent emissions could increase Manduca sexta pollination but also incur costs by increasing florivory or nectar robbing.
source: Since antagonists also use floral scent to locate host plants, increasing floral scent emissions would not only increased M. sexta pollination but could also incur costs by possibly increasing florivory or nectar robbing.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolutionary trade-offs of floral scent.

claim: Carpenter bees tend to rob more Nicotiana attenuata flowers on plants that emit benzylacetone than from plants that do not.
source: Carpenter bees, for example, tend to rob more N. attenuata flowers on plants that emit BA than from plants that do not (Kessler et al., 2008) and experimentally enhancing BA emissions increased rates of browsing (Baldwin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kessler et al., 2008 and Baldwin et al., 1997.

claim: Experimentally enhancing benzylacetone emissions increased rates of browsing in Nicotiana attenuata.
source: Carpenter bees, for example, tend to rob more N. attenuata flowers on plants that emit BA than from plants that do not (Kessler et al., 2008) and experimentally enhancing BA emissions increased rates of browsing (Baldwin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baldwin et al., 1997.

claim: The behavioral responses of each different pollinator to a given floral trait reinforce each other.
source: The differences between EV plants and SWEET9 as well as CHAL plants were maximized when plants were exposed to the entire community of pollinators at once, suggesting that the behavioral responses of each different pollinator to a given floral trait reinforce each other in ways that can only be understood through more detailed behavioral observations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that differences were maximized with the full pollinator community.

claim: Flowers visited by Manduca sexta contain a residual amount of nectar in the morning.
source: Unfortunately, we do not know if nectar secretion patterns change after flowers have been visited and nectar has been removed, but from nectar measurements, we know that flowers visited by M. sexta (which invariably removes the standing volume of nectar) again contain a residual amount of nectar in the morning.
evidence: This is based on nectar measurements from visited flowers.

claim: Manduca sexta invariably removes the standing volume of nectar when visiting flowers.
source: Unfortunately, we do not know if nectar secretion patterns change after flowers have been visited and nectar has been removed, but from nectar measurements, we know that flowers visited by M. sexta (which invariably removes the standing volume of nectar) again contain a residual amount of nectar in the morning.
evidence: This is based on observations of M. sexta feeding behavior.

claim: In the Silene latifolia–Hadena bicruris nursery pollination system, male moths provide a fitness benefit while interactions with females come with costs of seed-feeding caterpillars.
source: For example, in the Silene latifolia–Hadena bicruris nursery pollination system, male moths provide a fitness benefit for the plant, while interactions with females come with the substantial costs of seed-feeding caterpillars (Labouche and Bernasconi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Labouche and Bernasconi, 2009.

claim: Plants rarely interact with just one partner and usually face multiple selection pressures from mutualists and antagonists at the same time.
source: Plants rarely interact with just one partner and usually face multiple selection pressures from mutualists and antagonists at the same time, which may shape the different floral traits of a plant.
evidence: This is a general statement based on ecological knowledge.

claim: Pollinator networks are highly flexible and change frequently over time within a season.
source: Pollinator networks are known to be highly flexible and change frequently over time within a season (Olesen et al., 2008), as well as between years (Olesen et al., 2011) and this flexibility likely explains why plants recruit additional pollinator species rather than specialize if they rely on outcrossing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olesen et al., 2008 and 2011.

claim: Most pollinator networks are nested.
source: Most pollinator networks are nested (Pawar, 2014) and this nestedness is thought to stabilize mutualistic networks (Rohr et al., 2014), reducing interspecific competition and enhancing the number of coexisting species (Bastolla et al., 2009), with the end result of increasing the coexistence of several pollinating species on a plant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pawar, 2014, Rohr et al., 2014, and Bastolla et al., 2009.

claim: Nectar-free, pollinator cheating varieties of Nicotiana attenuata occur in nature.
source: Here, we demonstrate that nectar-free, pollinator cheating, varieties of N. attenuata occur in nature, and that producing no nectar can substantially reduce ovipositions by M. sexta, but that this comes with a reduction in pollination services.
evidence: This is supported by the screening data showing nectar-free plants in natural populations.

claim: Producing no nectar can substantially reduce ovipositions by Manduca sexta.
source: Here, we demonstrate that nectar-free, pollinator cheating, varieties of N. attenuata occur in nature, and that producing no nectar can substantially reduce ovipositions by M. sexta, but that this comes with a reduction in pollination services.
evidence: This is supported by oviposition data from SWEET9 plants.

claim: Producing no nectar comes with a reduction in pollination services.
source: Here, we demonstrate that nectar-free, pollinator cheating, varieties of N. attenuata occur in nature, and that producing no nectar can substantially reduce ovipositions by M. sexta, but that this comes with a reduction in pollination services.
evidence: This is supported by seed set data from SWEET9 plants.

claim: Cheating on nectar rewards works for one pollinator species but not for others.
source: While cheating on the nectar rewards works for one pollinator species, it does not for others.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses of H. lineata versus A. alexandri to nectar absence.

claim: Cheating with regards to floral scent has little influence on Manduca sexta oviposition but dramatically reduces outcrossing by Manduca sexta.
source: In contrast, cheating with regards to the attractant floral scent has little influence on M. sexta oviposition, but dramatically reduces outcrossing by M. sexta.
evidence: This is supported by comparing oviposition and seed set data from CHAL plants.

claim: All three examined pollinators show different responses to nectar and scent.
source: All three examined pollinators show different responses to nectar and scent and thus the interactions of multiple species are likely responsible for fine-tuning the evolution of both nectar and floral scent, as both H. lineata, as well as A. alexandri are important pollen vectors in the absence of M. sexta.
evidence: This is supported by the differential seed set results across the three pollinator species.

claim: Both nectar and floral scent in combination are required to maximize maternal fitness in nature particularly in ensuring Manduca sexta visitations.
source: Both traits in combination are required to maximize maternal fitness in nature particularly in ensuring M. sexta visitations, which we hypothesize delivers the greatest diversity of pollen genotypes compared to H. lineata and A. alexandri.
evidence: This is inferred from the seed set data showing CHALxSWEET9 plants had the lowest seed set.

claim: Manduca sexta delivers the greatest diversity of pollen genotypes compared to Hyles lineata and Archilochus alexandri.
source: Both traits in combination are required to maximize maternal fitness in nature particularly in ensuring M. sexta visitations, which we hypothesize delivers the greatest diversity of pollen genotypes compared to H. lineata and A. alexandri.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on M. sexta's movement patterns.

claim: The close association between Nicotiana attenuata and Manduca sexta may result from Manduca sexta's ability to move pollen over longer distances than other pollinators.
source: Hence, the close association between N. attenuata and M. sexta may result from M. sexta's ability to move pollen over longer distances than the other pollinators, and thus provide superior outcrossing services among N. attenuata populations which are frequently isolated by the large distances that frequently occur between fires, and hence N. attenuata populations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolutionary relationship between N. attenuata and M. sexta.

claim: Heterozygosity may increase herbivore resistance in future generations.
source: The long time between fires at any particular location may place a premium on outcrossing rates, as heterozygosity may increase herbivore resistance in future generations (Mescher et al., 2009; Bello-Bedoy and Nunez-Farfan, 2011), as well as longevity in the seedbank.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mescher et al., 2009 and Bello-Bedoy and Nunez-Farfan, 2011.

claim: Herbivores, as well as pollinators shape the evolution of floral traits.
source: We conclude that herbivores, as well as pollinators shape the evolution of floral traits and that it makes little sense to study floral traits as if they only mediate pollination services.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data showing both pollination and oviposition are affected by floral traits.

claim: It makes little sense to study floral traits as if they only mediate pollination services.
source: We conclude that herbivores, as well as pollinators shape the evolution of floral traits and that it makes little sense to study floral traits as if they only mediate pollination services.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the demonstrated dual effects of floral traits on both mutualists and antagonists.
